questions.domain: Domain 1: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management & Compliance (31%)
questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company wants to build an internal GenAI assistant that answers regulatory compliance questions across 18,000 FDA guidance PDFs updated weekly. Legal leadership requires inline citations pointing to the exact source document and page, and mandates zero model retraining when new regulations are published. Which adaptation strategy should the architect choose?
options: Paste the entire corpus of 18,000 PDFs into the system prompt of every Converse API request using Prompt Caching.
Run weekly Continued Pre-Training jobs in Amazon Bedrock on all 18,000 PDFs so the model memorizes the latest statutes.
Fine-tune a foundation model with Supervised Fine-Tuning every Friday using automatically generated question-answer pairs from the PDFs.
Implement Retrieval-Augmented Generation using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases backed by Amazon S3 and an OpenSearch Serverless vector store with incremental sync.
questions.explanation: Option D is correct because RAG with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases grounds answers in live S3 documents, provides native inline source citations, and updates incrementally in minutes via StartIngestionJob without retraining. Option B is wrong because Continued Pre-Training is expensive, slow, and cannot produce reliable document citations or handle weekly updates. Option C is wrong because Supervised Fine-Tuning is designed for style and format adaptation rather than dynamic factual recall. Option A is wrong because 18,000 PDFs vastly exceed any foundation model context window.
questions.use_case: Regulated life-sciences teams deploy Bedrock Knowledge Bases to serve auditable, cited answers over frequently changing FDA and EMA guidance documents.
questions.hack: Weekly changing facts + source citations + zero retraining = RAG via Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management & Compliance (31%)
questions.stem: A global manufacturing enterprise is ingesting 40,000 complex equipment service manuals into an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base. The PDFs contain dense multi-column wiring tables, schematics, and embedded flowcharts. After testing standard text chunking, engineers discover that table columns are scrambled and chart data is missing completely. Which AWS capability resolves this ingestion defect with minimal custom code?
options: Switch the embedding model from Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 to Cohere Embed English.
Reduce fixed-size chunk length from 500 tokens to 100 tokens with 50 percent overlap.
Enable Amazon Bedrock Data Automation or the Bedrock Foundation Model Parser during Knowledge Base ingestion to parse tables, charts, and visual layouts into structured text.
Convert all PDFs into raw Base64 strings and store them directly inside OpenSearch Serverless metadata fields.
questions.explanation: Option C is correct because Amazon Bedrock Data Automation and the Bedrock Foundation Model Parser visually analyze complex PDFs, preserving multi-column table geometry, diagrams, and charts as clean structured Markdown or JSON before chunking. Option B is wrong because smaller fixed chunks worsen scrambled text without fixing layout extraction. Option A is wrong because changing the embedding model cannot recover text or charts that the parser failed to extract. Option D is wrong because Base64 strings are not semantically searchable by vector embeddings.
questions.use_case: Industrial equipment makers use Bedrock Data Automation to index complex engineering schematics and multi-column maintenance tables accurately.
questions.hack: Scrambled PDF tables and missing charts in KB ingestion = Bedrock Data Automation or FM Parser.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management & Compliance (31%)
questions.stem: An insurance carrier's Knowledge Base indexes 12,000 multi-section policy handbooks. Engineers find that small 250-token fixed chunks match user queries accurately during vector search, yet the LLM frequently gives incomplete answers because critical policy exclusions sit in the adjacent paragraph. Larger 1,500-token chunks fix the context issue but cause retrieval precision to drop sharply. Which chunking strategy solves both problems simultaneously?
options: Configure Hierarchical Chunking in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases so small child chunks are indexed for high-precision retrieval while their larger parent chunks are passed to the foundation model.
Increase top-k retrieval from 5 to 60 small chunks and disable metadata filtering.
Switch from cosine similarity to Euclidean distance inside the vector database.
Disable chunking entirely and embed every 80-page handbook as a single vector record.
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because Hierarchical Chunking indexes fine-grained child chunks for precise semantic matching and automatically retrieves the encompassing parent chunk so the LLM receives complete surrounding exclusions and context. Option D is wrong because embedding entire 80-page handbooks dilutes semantic vectors and overflows context budgets. Option B is wrong because stuffing 60 tiny chunks triggers the Lost in the Middle effect and spikes input token costs. Option C is wrong because distance metrics cannot restore missing adjacent paragraphs.
questions.use_case: Insurance and legal RAG systems adopt Hierarchical Chunking to keep pinpoint search recall while delivering full clause context to the generator.
questions.hack: High precision of small chunks + full context of large chunks = Hierarchical Chunking.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management & Compliance (31%)
questions.stem: A FinTech company stores customer portfolio entitlements and account roles in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. The team wants to build a RAG assistant over financial research notes where every vector similarity query must execute an ACID-consistent SQL join against the live relational entitlement tables to enforce row-level access controls. Which vector store architecture fits best?
options: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless with a nightly AWS Glue export of Aurora entitlement tables.
Amazon Neptune Analytics GraphRAG synchronized via DynamoDB Streams.
Amazon S3 Vectors queried directly through Amazon Athena federated queries.
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension and an HNSW vector index.
questions.explanation: Option D is correct because Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector lets the application store embeddings alongside relational entitlement tables and execute single-query transactional SQL joins with HNSW vector search for real-time row-level security. Option A is wrong because nightly exports introduce up to 24 hours of stale authorization risk. Option C is wrong because S3 Vectors does not execute transactional ACID joins with Aurora tables. Option B is wrong because Neptune Analytics is designed for graph traversal rather than relational PostgreSQL entitlement joins.
questions.use_case: FinTech platforms leverage Aurora PostgreSQL pgvector when strict real-time relational RBAC joins must be combined with low-latency HNSW vector search.
questions.hack: Transactional SQL joins + existing relational RBAC + vectors = Aurora PostgreSQL pgvector with HNSW.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management & Compliance (31%)
questions.stem: A European supply-chain firm wants a GenAI system that uncovers hidden multi-hop risks across 25,000 supplier contracts, purchase orders, and logistics incident reports, such as identifying which Tier-1 electronics vendors indirectly depend on a disrupted Tier-3 mineral refiner. Standard flat vector search fails because no single document mentions both the Tier-1 vendor and the Tier-3 refiner. Which Bedrock Knowledge Bases architecture solves this?
options: Configure GraphRAG in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases backed by Amazon Neptune Analytics to extract and traverse entity relationships across documents.
Increase fixed chunk overlap to 40 percent inside Amazon OpenSearch Serverless.
Switch to a smaller 256-dimension embedding model with binary quantization.
Use Amazon S3 Select to run SQL LIKE queries across the raw contract PDFs.
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because GraphRAG with Amazon Neptune Analytics automatically builds a knowledge graph of entities and relationships across the entire corpus, enabling multi-hop traversal from Tier-1 vendors through Tier-2 sub-assemblies to Tier-3 refiners. Option B is wrong because chunk overlap only helps adjacent text inside a single document. Option D is wrong because S3 Select does not parse PDFs or perform multi-hop graph reasoning. Option C is wrong because reducing embedding dimensions saves memory but cannot link entities across separate files.
questions.use_case: Enterprise procurement and intelligence teams use Neptune Analytics GraphRAG to surface multi-hop vendor, legal, and compliance dependencies.
questions.hack: Multi-hop entity relationships across separate documents = GraphRAG with Amazon Neptune Analytics.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management & Compliance (31%)
questions.stem: A healthcare analytics company plans to fine-tune a foundation model on 80,000 clinical discharge summaries stored in Amazon S3. Before training begins, data engineers notice that 14 percent of records are near-duplicates copied across hospital transfers and several records contain unredacted patient Social Security Numbers. What must the engineering team do before launching the Bedrock fine-tuning job?
options: Split the dataset randomly first, then remove duplicates only from the training split while keeping them in validation.
Launch the fine-tuning job immediately and rely on Bedrock Guardrails at inference time to hide memorized SSNs.
Encrypt the S3 bucket with SSE-S3 and set temperature to 0.0 during fine-tuning so duplicates are ignored.
Run an AWS Glue pipeline with Amazon Comprehend PII detection to redact SSNs, deduplicate near-identical records before splitting train and validation sets, and enforce Glue Data Quality rules.
questions.explanation: Option D is correct because unredacted PII must be scrubbed upstream with Comprehend/Glue before training so the model never memorizes sensitive patient identifiers, and deduplication must happen before splitting to prevent train-validation data leakage and overfitting. Option B is wrong because allowing a custom model to memorize raw SSNs violates HIPAA and creates permanent data-extraction risk. Option C is wrong because SSE-S3 does not redact text content and temperature is an inference parameter. Option A is wrong because splitting before deduplication leaves near-duplicates leaking across splits.
questions.use_case: Healthcare ML teams run automated Glue + Comprehend PII scrubbing and MinHash deduplication pipelines prior to every Bedrock customization run.
questions.hack: PII + near-duplicates before fine-tuning = Glue + Comprehend PII redaction + deduplicate BEFORE train/val split.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management & Compliance (31%)
questions.stem: An e-commerce company wants to reduce its OpenSearch Serverless vector memory footprint by more than 60 percent across 40 million product descriptions without rebuilding its entire RAG architecture. Currently, the team embeds every product using 1,536-dimension float32 vectors. Which approach achieves this memory reduction with minimal impact on search recall?
options: Disable HNSW indexing and force full brute-force k-NN scans on every user query.
Re-index the corpus into a new vector index using Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 configured for 512 dimensions with vector quantization enabled.
Delete every second product chunk from the vector store and rely on the LLM to guess missing SKUs.
Truncate the existing 1,536-dimension float32 vectors in place without re-embedding future queries.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 supports Matryoshka configurable output dimensions (1024, 512, 256) and binary/int8 quantization, cutting RAM usage dramatically while preserving high semantic recall when the entire corpus is re-indexed cleanly into a new index. Option D is wrong because truncating arbitrary non-Matryoshka vectors and mixing dimensions breaks vector space compatibility. Option C is wrong because dropping products causes missing catalog results and hallucinations. Option A is wrong because brute-force scans destroy query latency without reducing stored vector size.
questions.use_case: High-volume retail catalogs migrate to 512-dim quantized Titan Embeddings V2 to slash OpenSearch Serverless OCU costs while keeping search quality high.
questions.hack: Cut vector RAM 60%+ with minimal recall loss = Titan Text Embeddings V2 lower dimensions (512/256) + quantization + full re-index.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management & Compliance (31%)
questions.stem: A media company maintains an archive of 250 million historical news embeddings that are queried only a few hundred times per day by investigative journalists. Keeping the entire 250-million-vector archive loaded in an always-on RAM-backed OpenSearch Serverless cluster costs thousands of dollars per month in idle OCU capacity. Which AWS vector storage option drastically lowers costs for this low-QPS massive archive?
options: Move the vectors into Amazon DynamoDB with Provisioned Read Capacity Units set to 10,000.
Provision an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL Global Database across three AWS Regions.
Store and query the embeddings using Amazon S3 Vectors for serverless, ultra-low-cost massive vector storage.
Migrate the 250 million embeddings to Amazon ElastiCache Redis cluster mode with 32 memory-optimized nodes.
questions.explanation: Option C is correct because Amazon S3 Vectors is purpose-built for massive-scale, cost-optimized serverless vector storage (tens of millions to billions of vectors) where always-on RAM vector databases incur excessive idle compute costs. Option D is wrong because storing 250 million vectors in ElastiCache RAM is even more expensive than OpenSearch Serverless. Option B is wrong because a multi-region Aurora Global Database adds unnecessary compute and replication costs. Option A is wrong because DynamoDB is a key-value store without native approximate nearest-neighbor vector indexing.
questions.use_case: Media archives and compliance repositories use Amazon S3 Vectors to store hundreds of millions of embeddings at a fraction of RAM-cluster cost.
questions.hack: Billions of vectors + low QPS + eliminate always-on RAM cost = Amazon S3 Vectors.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management & Compliance (31%)
questions.stem: A German banking group requires a customer-service GenAI application using Amazon Bedrock. Strict BaFin and GDPR mandates dictate that all customer prompts, completions, and RAG documents must remain exclusively within the European Economic Area, while operations still wants cross-region burst resilience to prevent single-region throttling. Which configuration satisfies both compliance and availability?
options: Configure a Global Cross-Region Inference Profile so traffic can burst to us-east-1 whenever Frankfurt is busy.
Host the application in us-east-1 and enable CloudFront Geo-Restriction to allow only German IP addresses.
Use single-region On-Demand invocation in eu-central-1 and instruct the model in the system prompt not to leave Europe.

Deploy all S3, KMS, and vector resources in eu-central-1, enforce an AWS Organizations SCP restricting aws:RequestedRegion to approved EU Regions, and invoke Bedrock via an EU Geographic Cross-Region Inference Profile.
questions.explanation: Option D is correct because an EU Geographic Cross-Region Inference Profile (eu.*) distributes burst capacity strictly across European AWS Regions (such as Frankfurt, Ireland, and Paris) without data ever leaving the EU, while the Organizations SCP guarantees regional data residency for S3, KMS, and vector stores. Option A is wrong because a Global profile can route traffic outside the EEA. Option B is wrong because CloudFront Geo-Restriction only filters client IPs and still processes banking data in the US. Option C is wrong because single-region On-Demand lacks cross-region burst resilience and system prompts do not control network routing.
questions.use_case: European financial institutions combine aws:RequestedRegion SCPs with EU Geographic CRIS profiles to achieve GDPR residency and multi-region burst capacity.
questions.hack: EU/GDPR residency + cross-region burst resilience = Geographic CRIS profile (eu.*) + aws:RequestedRegion SCP.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management & Compliance (31%)
questions.stem: A financial analytics team uploaded 120,000 rows of quarterly revenue CSV data into an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base using fixed-size text chunking. When executives ask for the exact sum of EMEA software revenue across Q1 through Q3, the assistant repeatedly outputs wrong totals. What is the architectural root cause and proper fix?
options: Top-k vector retrieval only fetches a handful of CSV chunks and cannot perform exact SQL aggregation; load the data into Amazon Redshift or AWS Glue Data Catalog and use Bedrock Knowledge Base Structured Data Retrieval (Text-to-SQL).
Increase chunk overlap to 30 percent and lower model temperature to 0.0 so the LLM adds numbers more accurately.
Convert the CSV file into a scanned PDF and re-ingest it with Amazon Bedrock Data Automation.
Switch to Hierarchical Chunking with 2,000-token parent chunks so more CSV rows fit in each vector.
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because vector similarity search retrieves only top-k fragments of a 120,000-row table and LLMs cannot accurately sum omitted rows; Structured Data Retrieval translates natural-language questions into exact SQL queries executed against Redshift or Glue Data Catalog/Athena. Option B is wrong because even at temperature 0.0, top-k retrieval misses 99 percent of the CSV rows. Option C is wrong because converting tabular CSV into PDF degrades structure without enabling SQL aggregation. Option D is wrong because 120,000 rows still cannot fit reliably in top-k parent chunks.
questions.use_case: Enterprise BI copilots route numeric aggregations over large tables to Redshift/Athena via Structured Data Retrieval rather than vector-chunking CSVs.
questions.hack: Exact SUM/AVG/COUNT over large CSV tables -> Structured Data Retrieval (Text-to-SQL), never raw vector chunking.

questions.stem: An engineering platform team builds a shared GenAI microservice that must invoke Amazon Nova Pro for routine summarization, Anthropic Claude for complex code review, and Meta Llama for open-weight experimentation. The team wants a single Python codebase supporting multi-turn chat, streaming, tool calling, and Guardrails without maintaining separate JSON request/response mappers per vendor. Which Bedrock API should they standardize on?
options: Amazon Bedrock CreateModelInvocationJob for synchronous chat requests.
Amazon SageMaker Runtime InvokeEndpoint with custom inference containers.
Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel and InvokeModelWithResponseStream with custom vendor payload adapters.
Amazon Bedrock Converse and ConverseStream unified APIs.
questions.explanation: Option D is correct because the Bedrock Converse and ConverseStream APIs provide a single consistent request and response schema across supported model providers for messages, system prompts, streaming, toolConfig, and guardrailConfig, allowing seamless model swaps via modelId. Option C is wrong because InvokeModel requires provider-specific payload schemas that break when switching vendors. Option B is wrong because SageMaker Runtime requires managing endpoints and custom adapters. Option A is wrong because CreateModelInvocationJob is for asynchronous offline batch processing.
questions.use_case: Multi-model platform teams standardize on Bedrock Converse so switching foundation models takes a single configuration change with zero schema rewrites.
questions.hack: Model-agnostic chat + streaming + tool use + guardrails across providers = Converse / ConverseStream.

questions.stem: A medical-device manufacturer maintains a RAG assistant over 90,000 engineering service bulletins filled with exact alphanumeric fault codes such as ERR-44B9-TX alongside conceptual troubleshooting paragraphs. Pure dense vector search retrieves general concepts well but misses exact fault codes, while pure keyword search misses conceptual synonyms. Engineers also notice that the top-5 results still include noisy tangential chunks. Which retrieval pipeline maximizes precision?
options: Enable Hybrid Search combining BM25 lexical matching and dense vector similarity in OpenSearch Serverless to fetch top-30 candidates, then pass them through the Amazon Bedrock Rerank API to select the top-5 passages.
Fine-tune the embedding model daily on every newly issued service bulletin.
Disable vector search entirely and use SQL LIKE queries in Amazon DynamoDB.
Use pure dense vector search with top-k set to 50 and ask the LLM in the prompt to ignore irrelevant chunks.
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because Hybrid Search captures both exact alphanumeric fault codes (via BM25 lexical search) and conceptual meaning (via dense vectors), and applying the cross-encoder Bedrock Rerank API re-scores the top-30 candidates deeply to surface the top-5 highest-precision passages. Option D is wrong because pure vector search misses exact SKU/fault codes and passing 50 noisy chunks degrades generation quality. Option C is wrong because DynamoDB does not support semantic search or BM25 ranking. Option B is wrong because daily embedding retraining requires full corpus re-indexing and is operationally prohibitive.
questions.use_case: Industrial and aerospace support assistants combine OpenSearch Hybrid Search with Bedrock Rerank to achieve >90% top-5 precision on fault-code manuals.
questions.hack: Exact alphanumeric codes + conceptual search + eliminate noisy top-k = Hybrid Search (top-30) + Bedrock Rerank (top-5).

questions.stem: A travel-booking platform uses the Amazon Bedrock Converse API to extract structured itinerary modifications (booking_id, departure_date, cabin_class enum) from free-form customer emails. Downstream parsers fail 6 percent of the time because the model wraps JSON in conversational preamble or markdown fences. How can the developer enforce strict JSON Schema adherence with minimal latency?
options: Define a single tool schema in Converse toolConfig matching the exact required JSON Schema and set toolChoice to force invocation of that specific tool.
Ask the model three times in the system prompt in uppercase letters to please output raw JSON only.
Increase model temperature to 0.8 and run a regex parser in a retry loop up to five times.
Switch to Amazon Bedrock Batch Inference so output formatting is validated offline.
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because passing a strict JSON Schema inside toolConfig with toolChoice set to that specific tool forces the model to emit a structured toolUse input block conforming to the schema without conversational preamble or markdown fences. Option C is wrong because higher temperature increases formatting randomness and retry loops waste tokens and latency. Option D is wrong because Batch Inference is asynchronous and does not enforce JSON schemas on its own. Option B is wrong because prompt-only requests remain probabilistic and still produce intermittent formatting drift.
questions.use_case: Backend extraction pipelines use forced toolChoice schemas in Converse to guarantee clean structured JSON payloads for downstream APIs.
questions.hack: Force strict schema-valid JSON in Converse -> toolConfig schema + forced toolChoice.

questions.stem: A wealth-management firm deploys an Amazon Bedrock Agent that can look up client portfolio balances and initiate wire transfers. Compliance policy mandates that the Agent may execute read-only balance lookups automatically, but any wire transfer above $1,000 must pause execution and return the proposed action parameters to the web application so an authenticated financial advisor can click Approve before funds move. Which Bedrock Agent feature directly supports this pattern?
options: Disable Action Groups completely and embed the wire-transfer API credentials inside the Knowledge Base.
Configure the wire-transfer Action Group with Return of Control (ROC) enabled so Bedrock pauses and returns the structured invocation payload to the calling application for human approval.
Enable Bedrock Agent Code Interpreter to execute the wire transfer inside a Python sandbox.
Grant the Agent Lambda execution role AdministratorAccess and instruct the Agent in its prompt to ask the user 'Are you sure?' in plain chat text.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because Return of Control (ROC) pauses the Bedrock Agent at the Action Group boundary and hands the exact structured action and parameters back to the host application, allowing deterministic UI confirmation and authorization before the backend executes the transfer and returns the result. Option D is wrong because relying on LLM conversational confirmation is vulnerable to prompt injection and violates least privilege. Option A is wrong because Knowledge Bases are read-only retrieval stores and must never hold credentials. Option C is wrong because Code Interpreter is an isolated math/data sandbox without direct banking API connectivity.
questions.use_case: Regulated financial and healthcare apps use Bedrock Agents Return of Control (ROC) to enforce deterministic human-in-the-loop approvals for high-risk writes.
questions.hack: Pause Bedrock Agent for human approval or client-side execution = Return of Control (ROC).

questions.stem: An enterprise IT organization built a single monolithic Bedrock Agent equipped with 38 Action Group tools spanning HR payroll, Jira incident management, AWS billing, and Salesforce CRM. In staging, the Agent frequently selects the wrong tool, hallucinates parameters, and exceeds token budgets due to massive OpenAPI schemas sent on every turn. What is the recommended architectural refactor?
options: Refactor into Amazon Bedrock Multi-Agent Collaboration with a Supervisor Agent delegating tasks to specialized Collaborator Agents (HR, IT Ops, FinOps, CRM), each scoped to its own small set of tools and least-privilege IAM role.
Combine all 38 OpenAPI endpoints into a single mega-endpoint named execute_everything with one untyped string parameter.
Increase maxTokens to 16,384 and set temperature to 1.0 so the Agent explores more tool combinations.
Remove all parameter descriptions from the OpenAPI schemas to shrink input token count.
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because Bedrock Multi-Agent Collaboration isolates specialized domains into focused Collaborator Agents with small, unambiguous toolsets and independent IAM boundaries, coordinated by a Supervisor Agent — slashing prompt bloat and dramatically improving tool-selection accuracy. Option B is wrong because an untyped mega-endpoint destroys schema validation and worsens parameter hallucination. Option C is wrong because higher temperature increases erratic tool choices. Option D is wrong because stripping parameter descriptions causes the LLM to guess argument semantics incorrectly.
questions.use_case: Large enterprises replace bloated single-agent designs with Bedrock Multi-Agent Collaboration to preserve tool accuracy and departmental least privilege.
questions.hack: 30+ tools causing schema bloat & wrong tool calls -> Bedrock Multi-Agent Collaboration (Supervisor + Collaborators).
